--- ABSTRACT ---
[BACKGROUND]: Intramedullary nailing is the treatment of choice for atypical femoral fractures. However, several problems, such as iatrogenic fracture and medial gap opening, can occur during intramedullary nailing when atypical femoral fractures are associated with excessive anterolateral bowing. To overcome these problems, we have developed a new grading system for anterolateral femoral bowing and a new technique for intramedullary nailing. The core of this new technique is matching the anterior curvature of the femoral nail with the anterolateral bowing of the femur when the nail passes the apex of the curvature, by rotating the nail externally.
[METHODS]: From January 2005 through March 2016, 24 female patients (30 cases) who underwent a surgical procedure for atypical femoral fracture with anterolateral bowing at 2 institutes were evaluated. The postoperative outcomes (anterolateral bowing grade, anterior and lateral bowing angles, medial gap and posterior gap of the fracture site, iatrogenic fracture, and time to initial medial callus formation and osseous union) were compared between the new technique (18 cases) and the conventional technique (12 cases).
[RESULTS]: With regard to the reliability of the new grading system, the interobserver and intraobserver reliability of the new grading system demonstrated an almost perfect agreement (kappainter = 0.893, kappaintra = 0.883). For patients with complete fractures, the differences between the preoperative and postoperative anterior and lateral bowing angles were significantly less (p = 0.013 for both) in the new technique group. The medial and posterior gaps at the fracture site were also significantly less in the new technique group (p = 0.013 for the medial gaps and p = 0.022 for the posterior gaps). Iatrogenic fracture occurred only in the conventional technique group, affecting 2 cases. The time to initial medial callus formation was significantly shorter (p = 0.033) in the new technique group compared with the conventional technique group.
[CONCLUSIONS]: Our new grading system for anterolateral femoral bowing is convenient and reliable. Furthermore, the new intramedullary nailing technique with the current intramedullary nail system is appropriate for the repair of atypical femoral fractures with excessive anterolateral bowing.

key_findings.finding: Radiographic/biomechanical simulation demonstrates nail–femur mismatch in severe bowing: in a 3D-printed femur (anterior curvature radius 772 mm; lateral bowing 15.4°), 8 of 9 tested commercial systems perforated the anterior cortex distally, and none achieved acceptable anatomic reduction; smaller-radius, smaller-diameter nails and specialized techniques improved theoretical fit.

Clinical AFF data show that bowing can cause reduction problems, medial gap opening, and iatrogenic fracture. In 30 cases, a nail-rotation technique matched nail curvature to anterolateral bowing, reduced medial/posterior fracture gaps, and had iatrogenic fractures only in the conventional-technique group (2 cases); medial callus formation was faster with the modified technique.

Alternative strategies are supported when standard rigid nails do not fit. In 20 patients/25 bowed AFFs (mean age 76.8), contralateral-side laterally bent nails achieved union in all cases without intraoperative or postoperative complications, with small residual gaps. A 77-year-old with bilateral severe bowing healed after elastic intramedullary nails, which were reported easier to insert than rigid nails. Plate fixation is another option when nails cannot be applied because of severe bowing; in 16 complete AFFs, all united, though short plates led to 2 later complete fractures at the plate end.

key_findings.finding: The available evidence supports a clinically important complication pathway—bowed elderly femur → nail mismatch/impingement or perforation and difficult reduction → iatrogenic fracture, residual gap/malalignment, or need for alternative implants/techniques. Evidence specifically labeled 'medial cortical impingement' is limited; most direct fit studies describe anterior cortical perforation, while the elderly insufficiency series specifically documents excessive medial bowing complicating nailing.

source_tools.relevance: Synthesis grounded in direct insufficiency, simulation, and clinical AFF evidence

entities.name: Medial bowing complicates nailing
observations: In a 4-patient elderly low-energy femoral insufficiency fracture series, excessive medial bowing was present in 6 femora and complicated intramedullary nail insertion; authors recommended long cephalomedullary nails. All fractures ultimately united.

source_tools.relevance: Direct evidence in elderly insufficiency fractures

entities.name: Bowing predicts iatrogenic fracture
observations: Among 95 women with atypical femoral fractures undergoing nailing, 20 (21.1%) sustained intraoperative iatrogenic fractures; lateral bowing was an independent predictor with an approximately 9.3-degree cutoff.

source_tools.relevance: Clinical outcome evidence linking bowing to nailing injury

entities.name: Nail-femur mismatch
observations: In a severe-bowing 3D femur simulation, 8 of 9 commercial nail systems perforated the distal anterior cortex and none achieved acceptable anatomic reduction; smaller-radius and smaller-diameter nails improved theoretical fit.

entities.name: Curvature-matched reduction
observations: In 30 atypical fracture cases, rotating the nail to match femoral curvature reduced medial/posterior fracture gaps and postoperative deformity; two iatrogenic fractures occurred in the conventional-technique group and none in the modified group.

source_tools.relevance: Clinical evidence for reduction difficulty and technique mitigation

entities.name: Alternative fixation for bowing
observations: Contralateral laterally bent nails achieved union in 25 bowed atypical femoral fractures without reported perioperative complications; elastic nails and long plates are additional options when rigid nails do not fit, whereas short plates were followed by fractures at plate ends in 2 cases.
